l: Odysseus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Odysseus was said to have lost his horses, found them at Pheneus, and considered keeping them there as he kept his oxen opposite Ithaca. He was also said to have built a temple to Artemis under the title Heurippe and offered a bronze statue of Poseidon Hippius, with the people of Pheneus claiming that his orders for the horse keepers were written on the statue's base. Pausanias doubted that Odysseus made the offering because bronze statues cast throughout were not known in that period.

l: Iphicles, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Iphicles, the brother of Hercules and father of Iolaus, was wounded while fighting with Hercules against Augeas and the people of Elis. His relations brought him to Pheneus, where Buphagus and Promne cared for him until he died of his wound and buried him. The people of Pheneus continued to honor him as a hero.

l: Hermes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The people of Pheneus paid special regard to Hermes, held games called Hermæa, and had a temple dedicated to him. His temple contained a stone statue made by the Athenian Euchir, son of Eubulides.

l: Myrtilus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Myrtilus was said to be the son of Hermes and the charioteer of Œnomaus. After betraying Œnomaus because of Pelops' promises, he was thrown from a ship by Pelops, and his body was washed ashore and buried by the people of Pheneus. They honored him annually at night, but Pausanias rejected the claim that the Myrtoan Sea was named after him.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Pheneus has a temple of Eleusinian Demeter where rites said to have been brought by Naus, great-grandson of Eumolpus, are celebrated in the manner of Eleusis. Near the temple is Petroma, two stones containing writings about the mysteries, which are read to initiates during the annual great rites. Beyond Pheneus are the ruins of a temple of Pythian Apollo, where the people still sacrifice to Apollo and Artemis and identify tombs associated with Hercules’ expedition against Elis. Mount Crathis contains the source of the river Crathis, which flows into the sea near Aegae and gave its name to a river in Italy.

l: Pheneus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Pheneus has a temple of Eleusinian Demeter and celebrates rites said to be like those at Eleusis. Its people maintain traditions about Demeter, Naus, Trisaules, and Damithales, and they still sacrifice to Apollo and Artemis at the ruins of the temple of Pythian Apollo.

l: Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Eleusinian Demeter has a temple at Pheneus. The people of Pheneus say that Naus came to them by order of the oracle at Delphi and brought the mysteries, and they also say that Demeter gave pulses other than beans to those who received her hospitably.

l: the Eleusinian Mysteries, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: The mysteries of Eleusinian Demeter were said by the people of Pheneus to have been brought there by Naus, the great-grandson of Eumolpus. They are celebrated at Pheneus in the same manner as at Eleusis.

l: Petroma, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Petroma consists of two large stones fitted together near the temple of Eleusinian Demeter. During the annual great rites, the stones are separated, writings about the rites are read to the initiated, and the stones are replaced that same night; many inhabitants of Pheneus regard “By Petroma” as their most solemn oath.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: The people of Pheneus still sacrifice to Pythian Apollo and Artemis at the site of the ruined temple. They say that Hercules built the temple after the capture of Elis.

l: the temple of Pythian Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: The temple of Pythian Apollo lies about 15 stades from Pheneus toward Pellene and Aegira, but only its ruins and a large white-stone altar remain. The people of Pheneus continue to sacrifice there to Apollo and Artemis, and tombs of heroes associated with Hercules’ expedition against Elis are nearby.

l: Hercules, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Hercules is said by the people of Pheneus to have built the temple of Pythian Apollo after capturing Elis. Heroes who joined his expedition against Elis are said to have been killed in the battle and buried near the temple.

l: the expedition against Elis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: The expedition against Elis is said to have been led by Hercules, with several heroes joining him and dying in the battle. The text argues that the famous Telamon and Chalcodon could not have taken part, suggesting instead that the buried men were obscure figures with the same names.

l: Mountain Crathis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Mount Crathis is the source of the river Crathis. It also contains a temple to Pyronian Artemis, from whose shrine the Argives formerly brought fire into the district around Lerne.

l: Crathis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: The river Crathis rises on Mount Crathis and flows into the sea near Aegae, which was once a town in Achaia but was deserted in the narrator’s time. A river in the district of the Bruttii in Italy received its name from this Crathis.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: East of Pheneus lies the promontory of Geronteum, which marks the boundary between Pheneus and Stymphelus. Near Geronteum are Tricrena, with three wells sacred to Hermes, and Sepia, where Æpytus son of Elatus died from a serpent bite and was buried. The serpents at Sepia are reduced by the annual snow and severe cold. The tomb of Æpytus is a modest earthen mound with a stone coping, which Pausanias was curious to see because Homer mentioned it.

l: Pheneus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Pheneus is the district reached when traveling eastward from it toward Geronteum and through which one passes after leaving Geronteum on the left. Geronteum forms its boundary with Stymphelus.

l: Geronteum, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Geronteum is a promontory east of Pheneus and has a road by it. It marks the boundary between the districts of Pheneus and Stymphelus.

l: Tricrena, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Tricrena is a group of mountains in the district of Pheneus, near Geronteum. It has three wells associated with the washing of Hermes after his birth.

l: wells (at Tricrena), Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The three wells at Tricrena are said to have been used by the mountain nymphs to wash Hermes when he was born. They are therefore considered sacred to Hermes.

l: Hermes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Hermes was said to have been washed by mountain nymphs in the three wells at Tricrena after his birth. The wells were consequently regarded as sacred to him.

l: Sepia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Sepia is a hill near Tricrena. It is said to be the place where Æpytus son of Elatus died from a serpent bite and was buried.

l: Æpytus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Æpytus, the son of Elatus, died on Sepia after being bitten by a serpent. His body was buried there because it could not be carried farther.

l: serpents (at Sepia), Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Serpents were said by the Arcadians still to inhabit Sepia, though not in great numbers. Annual snow kills those caught outside their holes and can also kill some inside when the bitter cold penetrates into them.

l: death of Æpytus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Æpytus died on Sepia from the bite of a serpent.

l: burial of Æpytus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Æpytus was buried on Sepia because those with him could not carry his dead body farther.

l: tomb of Æpytus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The tomb of Æpytus is a not very high earthen mound surrounded by a stone coping. Pausanias considered it notable because Homer had mentioned it, although it was less remarkable than other tombs he knew.

l: Homer, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Homer mentioned the tomb of Æpytus in his lines about the Arcadians. Pausanias thought Homer may have regarded it as remarkable because he had seen no more notable tomb.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Cyllene is described as the highest mountain in Arcadia and as the site of ruins of a temple of Cyllenian Hermes. The mountain and the god are said to have received their names from Cyllen, son of Elatus, while the statue of Cyllenian Hermes is made of juniper wood and is about eight feet high. Nearby Chelydorea marks the boundary between Pheneus and Pellene, and Nonacris lies near a cliff from which water called the Styx falls. Cyllene is also noted for its all-white blackbirds.

l: Cyllene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Cyllene is the highest of the mountains in Arcadia and contains the ruins of a temple of Cyllenian Hermes on its summit. Its name is said to derive from Cyllen, son of Elatus, and it is noted for blackbirds that are entirely white.

l: Hermes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Cyllenian Hermes has a ruined temple on the top of Mount Cyllene. His statue is made from juniper wood rather than ebony, cypress, cedar, oak, yew, or lotus, and is about eight feet high.

l: blackbirds of Mount Cyllene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The blackbirds of Mount Cyllene are all-white and lodge on the mountain. The text distinguishes them from birds called by the same name by the Bœotians, which are a different and non-vocal kind.

l: Chelydorea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Chelydorea is a mountain next to Cyllene, lying west of Pheneus. It is said to be the place where Hermes found the tortoise, and it forms the boundary between Pheneus and Pellene; the Achæans graze their flocks over most of it.

l: Pheneus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Pheneus is separated from Pellene by the mountain Chelydorea. From Pheneus, the westward road branches left toward Clitor and right toward Nonacris and the water of the Styx.

l: Nonacris, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Nonacris was formerly a small town in Arcadia named after the wife of Lycaon. In the present day it is in ruins, and even many parts of those ruins are difficult to trace.

l: Styx, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The Styx is the water that drops from a very high cliff near the ruins of Nonacris. The Greeks call this falling water the Styx.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Hesiod, Linus, and Epimenides describe Styx’s parentage and relationships, while Homer presents Styx in several poetic contexts, including as a river of Hades. Near Nonacris, water identified as the Styx drips from a cliff, flows into the Crathis, and is described as deadly and corrosive to many materials. Beyond Nonacris are the mountains Aroania, where the daughters of Prœtus reportedly hid after becoming mad. Melampus brought them to Lusi and cured them through sacrifices and purifications in the temple of Artemis, after which Artemis was called Hemerasia by the people of Clitor.

l: Hesiod, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Hesiod is said to have represented Styx in the Theogony as the daughter of Oceanus and the wife of Pallas.

l: Styx, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Styx is described in different traditions as the daughter of Oceanus and either the wife of Pallas or of Piras, to whom she bore Echidna. Homer presents Styx as a divine oath witness, as water flowing into the Titaresius, and as a river of Hades. Near Nonacris, its water drips from a cliff, flows into the Crathis, is deadly to humans and animals, and damages or melts many materials; a horse’s hoof is said to resist it.

l: Homer, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Homer frequently introduces Styx into his poetry. He depicts its water in Hera’s oath, has it flow into the Titaresius in a catalogue, and presents it as a river of Hades in Athene’s account of Hercules.

l: Nonacris, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Near Nonacris, water identified as the Styx drips from a cliff onto a lofty rock and then oozes into the river Crathis. The water is described as deadly and as having destructive effects on glass, crystal, stone, pottery, metals, and other materials.

l: Aroania, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Aroania consists of mountains beyond Nonacris that contain a cave. The daughters of Prœtus are said to have fled into this cave when they became mad.

l: daughters of Prœtus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The daughters of Prœtus fled into a cave in Aroania after becoming mad. Melampus brought them to Lusi and cured them through secret sacrifices and purifications in the temple of Artemis.

l: Melampus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Melampus brought the daughters of Prœtus from the cave in Aroania to Lusi. He cured them through secret sacrifices and purifications.

l: Lusi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Lusi was the place to which Melampus brought and cured the daughters of Prœtus. It was formerly a town on the borders of Clitor, but in the present time described in the text no ruins of it remain; its temple of Artemis was associated with the cure.

l: Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Artemis had a temple at Lusi where Melampus cured the daughters of Prœtus. Because of this event, the people of Clitor thereafter called Artemis Hemerasia.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Cynætha is an Arcadian town about 40 stades from the temple of Artemis, with a market-place containing altars and a statue of the Emperor Adrian. Its most memorable feature is a temple of Dionysus, where the inhabitants celebrate the god in winter by sacrificing a bull. A nearby well called Alyssus cures people bitten by mad dogs or otherwise injured when they drink its cold water. The road west from Pheneus toward Clitor follows the canal dug by Hercules and passes through Lycuria, the boundary between Pheneus and Clitor.

l: Cynætha, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Cynætha is inhabited by people of Arcadian race and lies about 40 stades from the temple of Artemis. Its market-place has altars of the gods and a statue of the Emperor Adrian, and its most memorable feature is a temple of Dionysus. A nearby well called Alyssus is said to cure people who drink its water after being bitten by a mad dog or receiving another injury.

l: Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Dionysus has a temple at Cynætha and a festival held there in wintertime. During the festival, men smeared with oil select a bull from the herd, believing that the god prompts them to take it to the temple for sacrifice.

l: temple of Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The temple of Dionysus is the most memorable feature of Cynætha. During the god's winter festival, a bull is brought there and offered in sacrifice.

l: festival of Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The festival of Dionysus at Cynætha takes place in wintertime. Men smeared all over with oil pick a bull from the herd and convey it to the temple, where it is sacrificed.

l: well Alyssus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The well Alyssus lies about two stades from Cynætha, with a plane-tree growing beside it. Its cold water is believed to cure people bitten by mad dogs or suffering from another injury.

l: water of Alyssus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The water of Alyssus is cold and is said to cure people who drink it after being bitten by a mad dog or receiving another hurt. It is contrasted with the water called Styx near Pheneus, which is harmful to people.

l: Pheneus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Pheneus has the water called Styx near it, which is harmful to people. A westward road from Pheneus leads toward Clitor along the canal dug by Hercules for the river Aroanius, passing through Lycuria.

l: Styx, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Styx is the name of the water near Pheneus. Unlike the water at Cynætha, it is said to be harmful to people.

l: Clitor, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Clitor is reached by a westward road from Pheneus that runs along the canal dug by Hercules for the river Aroanius. Lycuria marks the boundary between the districts of Clitor and Pheneus.

l: Lycuria, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Lycuria lies along the road from Pheneus to Clitor beside the canal dug by Hercules for the river Aroanius. It is the boundary between the districts of Pheneus and Clitor.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The text describes the springs of the river Ladon, which are said to be formed when water from the marsh at Pheneus reappears after passing beneath the mountains. It praises the Ladon for the beauty of its stream and connects it with the story of Daphne. According to traditions in Arcadia and Elis, Leucippus, son of Œnomaus, disguised himself as a woman to pursue Daphne, who disliked men. When Daphne and the other maidens bathed in the Ladon, they discovered Leucippus's sex and killed him, while poets attribute his death to Apollo's jealousy.

l: springs of the river Ladon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The springs are reached about 50 stades from Lycuria. It is said that water from the marsh at Pheneus, after falling into pits beneath the mountains, reappears there and forms the springs, though the text does not confirm whether this is true.

l: Ladon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The Ladon is said to surpass all the rivers in Greece for the beauty of its stream. It is also famous in connection with what poets have sung about Daphne.

l: Daphne, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Daphne is associated with a tradition preserved in Arcadia and Elis. She disliked all males, befriended Leucippus while believing him to be a girl, and later bathed in the Ladon with the other maidens.

l: Œnomaus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Œnomaus was the ruler at Pisa and the father of Leucippus. Leucippus claimed while disguised that he was Œnomaus's daughter.

l: Leucippus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Leucippus, son of Œnomaus, fell in love with Daphne and pursued her despite her dislike of males. He disguised himself as a girl, gained Daphne's friendship, and was later discovered and killed by Daphne and the other maidens.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: According to those who sing of Apollo's love for Daphne, Apollo was jealous of Leucippus's happiness in love.

l: Apollo's love for Daphne, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Poets connect Apollo's love for Daphne with the story of Leucippus. They add that Apollo's jealousy of Leucippus contributed to the circumstances of Leucippus's death.

l: Leucippus's disguise, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Leucippus let his hair grow to the Alpheus, wore women's dress, arranged his hair like a girl's, and claimed to be Œnomaus's daughter. He joined Daphne in hunting and was accepted as a girl because of his appearance, family distinction, hunting skill, and attention to her.

l: bathing and swimming in the Ladon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Daphne and the other maidens wished to bathe and swim in the Ladon. They stripped Leucippus against his will during this activity and discovered his sex.

l: Leucippus's killing, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: After discovering that Leucippus was male, Daphne and the other maidens stabbed and killed him with javelins and daggers. The account also says that poets attribute the episode to Apollo's jealousy.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The road from the springs of Ladon to the town of Clitor is 60 stades and follows the Aroanius through a narrow path. Near Clitor, the river Clitor joins the Aroanius about 7 stades from the town. The Aroanius contains several kinds of fish, including variegated fish said to sound like thrushes. Clitor has temples to Demeter, Æsculapius, and Ilithyia, as well as other sanctuaries nearby.

l: Ladon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The springs of Ladon are 60 stades from the town of Clitor by a narrow road along the Aroanius.

l: Aroanius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The Aroanius runs beside the road from the springs of Ladon to Clitor. It receives the river Clitor about 7 stades from the town and contains various fish, including variegated fish said to have a voice like the thrush.

l: town of Clitor, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The town of Clitor lies in a plain surrounded by low hills and takes its name from the son of Azan. It has notable temples to Demeter, Æsculapius, and Ilithyia, and a temple to Castor and Pollux under the name of the Great Gods about 4 stades away; a temple and statue of Athene Coria stand about 30 stades away on a hilltop.

l: Ilithyia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The town of Clitor has a notable temple to Ilithyia. Homer says there are several Ilithyias without specifying their number, while the Lycian Olen identifies her with Fate, says she is older than Cronos, and calls her Eulinus.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Stymphelus lies at the boundary between Pheneus and Stymphelus and, though no longer ranked as Arcadian, is said to be Arcadian by race. Its spring forms the river Stymphelus in winter, and the river disappears underground before emerging in Argolis as the Erasinus. Stymphelus is associated with man-eating birds called Stymphelides, whom Hercules was said either to have killed with arrows or frightened away with rattles. The town also has an ancient temple of Stymphelian Artemis, and a later disruption of the river was interpreted as punishment for neglecting her festival.

l: Stymphelus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Stymphelus is no longer ranked as Arcadian but belongs to the Argolic League by its own choice. Homer and the ancestry of its founder, Stymphelus, are said to testify that its people are Arcadian by race. The town has a spring, an ancient temple of Stymphelian Artemis, and traditions about man-eating birds.

l: spring at Stymphelus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The spring at Stymphelus was used by the Emperor Adrian to convey water to Corinth. In winter it turns a small marsh into the river Stymphelus, while in summer the river is fed only by the spring.

l: river Stymphelus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The river Stymphelus flows from the spring, soaks into the ground, and reemerges in Argolis under the name Erasinus. A tree once blocked the place where it went underground, turning the plain into a marsh for 400 stades until a fleeing deer and a pursuing hunter entered the swamp and, according to the story, opened a way for the water.

l: Stymphelian birds, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Man-eating birds were said to have lived on the banks of the river Stymphelus. Hercules was said to have killed them with his arrows, though Pisander of Camirus said that he only frightened them away with the noise of rattles.

l: Hercules, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Hercules was said to have dealt with the man-eating birds of Stymphelus. One tradition says that he killed them with arrows, while Pisander of Camirus said that he frightened them away with rattles.

l: Arabia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Arabia is said to contain savage birds called Stymphelides, which attack and kill people and can pierce coats of mail and thick robes of mat. The text suggests that birds formerly associated with Stymphelus may have flown from Arabia, though their appearance and original Arabian name are uncertain.

l: Stymphelides, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The Stymphelides in Arabia are described as birds about the size of cranes, resembling storks but having stronger, non-crooked beaks. They are savage toward humans and can pierce armor and thick robes. Birds with the same name were represented on the roof of the temple of Stymphelian Artemis.

l: Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Stymphelian Artemis had an ancient temple at Stymphelus. Her festival was once celebrated negligently and with violations of established custom, after which the river was blocked and the plain flooded; since the water was released, the festival has been celebrated with greater ardour.

l: temple of Stymphelian Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The temple of Stymphelian Artemis at Stymphelus contains a wooden statue that is mostly gilt. Its roof shows representations of the Stymphelides, and some maidens carved in white stone with bird-like legs stand behind it.

l: festival of Stymphelian Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The festival of Stymphelian Artemis was once celebrated at Stymphelus rather negligently and in violation of much of its established routine. After the river was blocked and the plain flooded, the festival was celebrated with greater ardour.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The unit describes Alea, Caphyæ, and the surrounding roads, waterways, sanctuaries, and settlements in Arcadia. It records traditions about Cepheus, Menelaus, and the origin of Caphyæ, including Menelaus’ plane-tree and well. It also explains how Artemis of Condylea became known as Apanchomene after children were stoned and a disorder afflicted the women of Caphyæ. The route continues past Nasi and Ladon through Soron to the boundary of Clitor and Psophis at Siræ.

l: Alea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Alea is a town in the Argolic league, said to have been founded by Aleus the son of Aphidas. It has temples of Ephesian Artemis and Alean Athene, and a temple and statue of Dionysus.

l: Scieria, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Scieria is the annual festival of Dionysus celebrated at Alea. During it, women are flogged according to an oracle from Delphi, as Spartan boys are flogged at the temple of Orthia.

l: Orchomenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Orchomenus is connected to Caphyæ by a straight road through a ravine and by another road on the left of the lake. Water from its territory is held in a reservoir in the plain of Caphyæ.

l: Caphyæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Caphyæ lies at the end of a plain beneath low hills and is named clearly from Cepheus, though the Arcadian dialect has produced the name Caphyæ. Its inhabitants say they came from Attica after Ægeus expelled them from Athens and that they sought refuge from Cepheus; the town has temples of Poseidon and Cnacalesian Artemis.

l: reservoir near Caphyæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The reservoir in the plain of Caphyæ holds back water from the territory of Orchomenus so that it will not damage the fertile district. Within it, another body of water nearly as large as a river is absorbed into the ground.

l: Nasi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Nasi is the place near the village of Rheunos where water from the reservoir reemerges. It is reached by descending after ascending seven stades from Caphyæ.

l: Cepheus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Cepheus is the son of Aleus and is said to have given Caphyæ its name. The inhabitants of Caphyæ reportedly supplicated him to let them settle there after they fled from Athens.

l: Arcadia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Arcadia is the region to which the inhabitants of Caphyæ say they fled after being expelled from Athens. Its dialect is said to account for the form of the name Caphyæ.

l: Menelaus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Menelaus is said to have come to Caphyæ while mustering his army against Troy. According to local tradition, he planted a plane-tree beside the well there.

l: Menelaus' plane-tree, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Menelaus' plane-tree stands beside a well above Caphyæ, and both the tree and the well bear his name. The text calls it the most ancient of the other trees mentioned, if Greek traditions about ancient living trees are credible.

l: Condylea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Condylea is about a stade from Caphyæ and formerly had a grove and temple dedicated to Artemis of Condylea. It is associated with the story explaining the goddess's changed title.

l: Artemis of Condylea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Artemis of Condylea was given the title Apanchomene after children playing near her temple tied a rope around her statue's neck and said they would strangle her. The people of Caphyæ stoned the children, and an oracle later ordered rites for them because they had not been justly slain.

l: children of Caphyæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The children came across a rope while playing near the temple of Artemis of Condylea and tied it around the statue's neck. The people of Caphyæ stoned them, after which the Pythian Priestess said they had been unjustly slain and ordered that they be buried and honored annually.

l: people of Caphyæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The people of Caphyæ stoned the children who had placed a rope around the statue of Artemis of Condylea. They obeyed the Pythian Priestess by burying the children and continuing to perform funeral rites for them annually.

l: strange disorder at Caphyæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: A strange disorder afflicted the women of Caphyæ after the children were stoned. The women prematurely gave birth to dead children until the Pythian Priestess gave an explanation and prescribed rites for the stoned children.

l: Pythian Priestess, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The Pythian Priestess said that the children stoned by the people of Caphyæ had not been slain justly. She instructed the people to bury them and perform funeral rites for them annually.

l: Apanchomene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Apanchomene, meaning strangled, became the title used for Artemis after the children tied a rope around her statue's neck. The people of Caphyæ attributed this title to the oracle.

l: funeral rites for the stoned children, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The funeral rites were ordered by the Pythian Priestess for the children stoned by the people of Caphyæ. The people obeyed the instruction and continued to perform the rites annually.

l: Ladon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The river Ladon lies fifty stades beyond Nasi. After crossing it, the traveler reaches the oak-coppice Soron.

l: Soron, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Soron is an oak-coppice between Argeathæ, Lycuntes, and Scotane, on the road to Psophis. Its oak-coppices shelter wild animals such as boars and bears, as well as immense tortoises whose shells could make very large lyres; the ruins of Paus lie at its end.

l: Psophis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Psophis is reached by the road through Soron. The boundary between the districts of Clitor and Psophis is at Siræ.

l: Siræ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Siræ is a place near the end of Soron and marks the boundary between the districts of Clitor and Psophis.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The unit describes the competing traditions about the founding and naming of Psophis, including its connection with Phegia, Hercules, and Erymanthus. It recounts the Erymanthian boar hunt, the ruined temple of Aphrodite Erycina, and the burial place of Alcmæon at Psophis. Alcmæon’s exile, marriages, pursuit of the necklace of Eriphyle, and treacherous death are linked to Delphi, Achelous, and the origins of the Acarnanians. The account concludes by questioning the tradition that Aglaus of Psophis enjoyed uninterrupted happiness and reflecting on human fortune and misfortune.

l: Psophis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Psophis is associated with several founding traditions, including Psophis the son or daughter of named ancestors and Psophis, the daughter of Eryx. The settlement was formerly called Phegia, and Echephron and Promachus changed its name to Psophis after their mother. It lies near Siræ, the Aroanius, and the Erymanthus, and contains sanctuaries, hero-chapels, and the tomb of Alcmæon.

l: Phegia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Phegia was the former name of Psophis and was said to have been called Erymanthus before the reign of Phegeus. Lycortas dwelt there and brought up Echephron and Promachus, the sons of Hercules and Psophis. Alcmæon married Alphesibœa, the daughter of Phegeus, while the town was still called Phegia.

l: Hercules, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Hercules fathered Echephron and Promachus by Psophis. At the orders of Eurystheus, he hunted the Erymanthian boar on the banks of the Erymanthus.

l: Erymanthus (river), Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Erymanthus flows by Psophis after rising in Mount Lampea, which is sacred to Pan and may form part of Mount Erymanthus. It passes through Arcadia, leaving Mount Pholoe on the right and Thelpusa on the left, and becomes a tributary of the Alpheus. The people of Psophis have a temple and statue dedicated to the River-God Erymanthus on its banks.

l: Erymanthian boar, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Erymanthian boar was said to exceed all other boars in size and strength. Hercules hunted it on the banks of the Erymanthus, while the people of Cumæ claimed that boar’s teeth kept in Apollo’s temple were its teeth, a claim the account considers improbable.

l: Aphrodite, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Psophis has a temple of Aphrodite Erycina that is now in ruins and was reportedly built by the sons of Psophis. The account connects this sanctuary with the ancient and wealthy temple of Aphrodite Erycina near Mount Eryx in Sicily.

l: Alcmæon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Alcmæon, the son of Amphiaraus, is buried at Psophis beneath a tomb shaded by sacred cypress trees called Maidens. After killing his mother, he fled Argos, married Alphesibœa at Phegia, and later consulted Delphi because his madness did not improve. He eventually settled on land formed by the Achelous, married Callirhoe, and was treacherously killed after returning to Phegia in pursuit of the necklace of Eriphyle.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Delphi was consulted by Alcmæon when his madness continued during his residence in Arcadia. The sons of Phegeus were said to have offered the necklace of Eriphyle to Apollo at Delphi.

l: Achelous, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Achelous formed new land by silting, and Alcmæon settled there after learning from Delphi that he would be safe on ground created after his mother’s bloodshed. Alcmæon married Callirhoe, the daughter of Achelous, and the account attributes the separation of the Echinades from the mainland to changes in the river’s deposits.

l: Eriphyle, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Eriphyle was Alcmæon’s mother, whom he killed before fleeing Argos. The prophecy concerning Alcmæon stated that the Avenger of his mother Eriphyle would pursue him except on land newly formed by the sea.

l: necklace of Eriphyle, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The necklace of Eriphyle was among the gifts Alcmæon gave to Alphesibœa. Callirhoe desired it and sent Alcmæon unwillingly to Phegia to obtain it; Temenus and Axion treacherously caused his death, and they were said to have offered the necklace to Apollo at Delphi.

l: Aglaus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Aglaus was a native of Psophis and a contemporary of the Lydian Crœsus. The account rejects the local tradition that he was happy throughout his life.

l: oracle at Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The oracle at Delphi told Alcmæon that the Avenger of his mother Eriphyle would follow him everywhere except onto land most recently created by the sea. It also informed Aglaus that he would experience both good and bad fortune.

l: human fortune and misfortune, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The account argues that one person may suffer less trouble than another, but that no person can remain entirely free from misfortune. It compares human experience to ships facing different degrees of storm and to Homer’s two jars, one filled with blessings and the other with woes.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The road from Psophis to Thelpusa passes Tropæa, Aphrodisium, the boundary pillar, and several sites associated with rivers and temples. Thelpusa lies on a lofty ridge by the Ladon and contains temples of Æsculapius, the twelve gods, and Eleusinian Demeter. The text describes Demeter’s pursuit by Poseidon, her transformation into a mare, and her later worship as Erinys and Lusia at Onceum. It also recounts traditions about Arion, the divine horse, and Æsculapius’s exposure and upbringing near Thelpusa.

l: Psophis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Psophis is the starting point of the road to Thelpusa. A pillar with ancient writing marks the boundary between the territories of Psophis and Thelpusa.

l: Thelpusa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Thelpusa is about 40 stades from the temple of Causian Æsculapius and is said to have been named after the River-Nymph Thelpusa, daughter of Ladon. It stands on a lofty ridge by the Ladon, has few inhabitants, and contains temples of Æsculapius, the twelve gods, and Eleusinian Demeter. Thelpusa is also associated with the worship of Demeter as Erinys and Lusia and with the exposure of Æsculapius.

l: Ladon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Ladon rises near Clitor and flows through several places before reaching Thelpusa, where it passes the temple of Eleusinian Demeter. It then flows past the temple of Demeter at Onceum and other sanctuaries before joining the Alpheus at the Island of Crows. Though renowned for its beauty, it is not wide enough to form navigable islands.

l: temple of Demeter and Proserpine, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The temple of Eleusinian Demeter stands near Thelpusa beside the Ladon. It contains stone statues of Demeter, Proserpine, and Dionysus, each no less than seven feet high.

l: Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: While searching for Proserpine, Demeter changed herself into a mare to escape Poseidon and grazed with the horses at Onceum. After Poseidon pursued and united with her in horse form, she became furious but later bathed in the Ladon. She was worshipped at Thelpusa as Erinys, meaning Fury, and as Lusia, associated with her bathing; her wooden statues had Parian-marble heads, fingers, and toes.

l: Onceum, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Onceum is a place in Thelpusa where Oncius, the son of Apollo, was said to have ruled. It was also the location of the grove of Oncean Apollo and the sanctuary associated with Demeter Erinys.

l: temple of Demeter at Onceum, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The Ladon flows from Thelpusa toward the temple of Demeter at Onceum. The people of Thelpusa call the goddess worshipped there Erinys, and traditions connect the sanctuary with Demeter’s encounter with Poseidon.

l: Poseidon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Poseidon pursued Demeter with amatory intent while she searched for Proserpine. He changed himself into a horse after discovering her transformation into a mare and united with her; he was consequently called Hippius there first in Arcadia.

l: the amour of Poseidon with Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Demeter’s union with Poseidon occurred after she changed into a mare and Poseidon changed into a horse at Onceum. The tradition says that Demeter bore a daughter whose name was not revealed to the uninitiated and the foal Arion.

l: Arion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Arion was a swift, dark-maned horse associated with Poseidon and Demeter, although Antimachus said that he was born from the earth near the grove of Oncean Apollo. Hercules reportedly rode Arion against the people of Elis after obtaining the horse from Oncus, and later gave him to Adrastus, who was said to have been the third to break him in.

l: Æsculapius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Æsculapius has a temple at Thelpusa, as well as a temple of the Boy Æsculapius near the Ladon. The boy was said to have been exposed at Thelpusa, found by Autolaus, the bastard son of Arcas, and brought up by him; the latter story is given as the reason for the temple. The temple also contains the tomb of Trygon, said to have been Æsculapius’s nurse.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Heræa, founded by Heræus son of Lycaon, lies along the Alpheus and contains race-courses, baths, temples, and other religious buildings. Its athlete Damaretus was the first to win at Olympia in the race in heavy armour. The route from Heræa toward Elis crosses the Ladon and the Erymanthus, whose boundary status is disputed between Arcadian and Eleian accounts. Aliphera, named for Alipherus son of Lycaon, lies beyond the Alpheus and has notable temples and a bronze statue of Athene, while nearby Melæneæ is deserted and Buphagium marks the sources of the Buphagus.

l: Heræa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Heræa was founded by Heræus son of Lycaon and lies mostly on a gentle eminence on the right of the Alpheus, with part of the town extending to the river. It has race-courses, baths, temples of Dionysus, a building for the orgies of Dionysus, a temple of Pan, and ruins of a temple of Hera. Damaretus of Heræa was the foremost of the Arcadian athletes and the first victor at Olympia in the race in heavy armour.

l: Alpheus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The Alpheus lies beside Heræa, and travelers cross it when going from Heræa to Aliphera. The Buphagus falls into the Alpheus.

l: Arcadia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Arcadia is associated with Heræa, whose founder was the son of Lycaon, and Pan is said to have been a native of Arcadia. According to the Arcadian account, the Erymanthus is the boundary between Heræa and Elis.

l: Olympia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Damaretus of Heræa was the first victor at Olympia in the race in heavy armour. Corœbus was the first victor at Olympia after Iphitus restored the games, according to the inscription on his tomb.

l: Elis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The route from Heræa to Elis crosses the Ladon and then reaches the Erymanthus. The boundary between Heræa and Elis is identified as the Erymanthus by the Arcadian account, while the people of Elis identify it as the tomb of Corœbus.

l: Erymanthus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The Erymanthus lies about 20 stades from the Ladon on the route from Heræa to Elis. According to the Arcadian account, it forms the boundary between Heræa and Elis.

l: Corœbus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Corœbus was victor when Iphitus restored the Olympian games after they had long been discontinued, when prizes were offered only for racing. An inscription on his tomb calls him the first victor at Olympia.

l: tomb of Corœbus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The tomb of Corœbus was erected on the borders of Elis. The people of Elis say that it marks the boundary between Heræa and Elis.

l: restoration of the Olympian games, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The restoration of the Olympian games is associated with Iphitus, who restored them after they had been discontinued for a long time. At the restoration, prizes were offered only for racing, and Corœbus was the victor.

l: Olympian games, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The Olympian games had been discontinued for a long time before Iphitus restored them. When they were restored, prizes were offered only for racing.

l: Aliphera, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Aliphera was a small town that many inhabitants abandoned when the Arcadian colony was formed at Megalopolis. Named for Alipherus son of Lycaon, it has temples of Æsculapius and Athene, an altar to Zeus Lecheates, the fountain Tritonis, and a notable bronze statue of Athene by Hypatodorus. Its people hold a public festival at which they first sacrifice to Muiagrus, whom they invoke against flies.

l: Megalopolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Megalopolis received an Arcadian colony at the time when many inhabitants abandoned Aliphera. Buphagium and the sources of the Buphagus lie on the boundary between the districts of Megalopolis and Heræa.

l: Athene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Athene is worshipped especially at Aliphera, where the inhabitants say that she was born and reared. Aliphera has a temple and a notable bronze statue of Athene by Hypatodorus, and its public festival is thought to be dedicated to her.

l: Buphagus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The Buphagus rises at Buphagium and falls into the Alpheus. Its sources form the boundary between the districts of Megalopolis and Heræa.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Megalopolis was founded in Arcadia soon after the Lacedæmonians’ defeat at Leuctra, with Epaminondas the Theban encouraging the Arcadians to unite and sending 1,000 Thebans for their protection. The city resisted Lacedæmonian attacks, defeated an army led by Acrotatus, and later joined the Achæan League under the leadership of Lydiades. Cleomenes eventually captured Megalopolis in peacetime, killed many inhabitants, drove out others, and destroyed the city, while Philopœmen saved many of its men and boys and led them with the women to Messenia. The unit also identifies the boundary between Megalopolis and Heræa as the source of the river Buphagus.

l: Megalopolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Megalopolis was founded as a recent city of Arcadia by gathering inhabitants from many Arcadian towns, and it became strong through its alliance with Thebes. Its people resisted Lacedæmonian attacks, defeated Acrotatus, later joined the Achæan League, and were eventually defeated and expelled when Cleomenes captured and destroyed the city.

l: Arcadia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: The Arcadians crowded into Megalopolis to strengthen themselves against the Lacedæmonians, following the example of Argos. Most Arcadian towns accepted the plan, though the people of Lycæatæ, Tricolonus, Lycosura, and Trapezus resisted, with some being forced into Megalopolis and the people of Trapezus leaving the Peloponnese.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: The Lacedæmonians tried to prevent the colonization of Megalopolis and later repeatedly attacked it. They were defeated under Acrotatus, defeated the Megalopolitans under Agis but failed to capture the city when the North Wind shattered Agis’ battering-ram, and ultimately captured Megalopolis under Cleomenes.

l: Epaminondas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Epaminondas the Theban was regarded as the founder of Megalopolis because he stirred the Arcadians to colonize the city. He sent 1,000 picked Thebans under Parmenes to defend the Arcadians if the Lacedæmonians tried to stop the colonization.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: The Thebans supported the founding of Megalopolis by sending 1,000 picked men under Parmenes to protect the Arcadians. Megalopolis was enrolled in alliance with Thebes, and the city initially believed that this alliance removed its fear of the Lacedæmonians.

l: Macedonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: The hostility between the Arcadians and the Lacedæmonians increased the power of the Macedonians and Philip the son of Amyntas. The Arcadians did not fight on the side of the Greeks at Chæronea or in Thessaly.

l: Aristodemus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Aristodemus, a Phigalian and the son of Artylas, seized the chief power in Megalopolis after being adopted by Tritæus. Although he ruled alone, he was called Good man and True, and during his rule Megalopolis defeated the Lacedæmonians under Acrotatus.

l: Cleomenes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Cleomenes the son of Leonidas captured Megalopolis in time of peace. He killed the inhabitants he captured, razed the city to the ground, and burned it, while the account also notes that he had changed the Lacedæmonian constitution from a kingdom to an autocracy.

l: Lydiades, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Lydiades seized the chief power in Megalopolis two generations after the death of Aristodemus. Though ambitious, he voluntarily abdicated when he reached maturity, and after Megalopolis joined the Achæan League he was honored by his city and the Achæans as highly as Aratus. He later fell fighting during the capture of Megalopolis.

l: Achæan League, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Megalopolis joined the Achæan League, after which Lydiades was held in high honor by the Achæans. His fame was considered equal to that of Aratus.

l: Philopœmen, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Philopœmen the son of Craugis saved about two-thirds of the lads and grown men of Megalopolis when Cleomenes captured the city. He fled with them and the women to Messenia.

l: Leuctra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: The colonization of Megalopolis took place a year and a few months after the reverse of the Lacedæmonians at Leuctra. The city was colonized in the second year of the 102nd Olympiad, when Phrasiclides was Archon at Athens and Damon of Thuria won the course.

l: Arcadian colony at Megalopolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: The colonization gathered numerous Arcadian towns and their inhabitants into Megalopolis so that Arcadia would be stronger against the Lacedæmonians. Epaminondas the Theban promoted the plan, Thebans provided military protection, and most of Arcadia joined, although some communities resisted and suffered expulsion or forced relocation.

l: capture and destruction of Megalopolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Cleomenes captured Megalopolis in time of peace, and some inhabitants who defended the city at night were driven out while Lydiades was killed in the fighting. Cleomenes killed those he captured, razed the city, and burned it, while Philopœmen saved many of the men and boys and led them with the women to Messenia.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Gortys is described as a former town and present-day village with a temple of Æsculapius and statues by Scopas. Its river, called Lusius locally and Gortynius elsewhere, is said to be exceptionally cold and to rise at Thisoa before joining the Alpheus. Nearby Teuthis, formerly a town, is associated with the Arcadian leader Teuthis, who wounded Athene and was later punished by a wasting disease. A monument near the road from Gortys to Megalopolis commemorates those who died in the battle against Cleomenes.

l: Gortys, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Gortys is a village in the narrator's day but was formerly a town. It contains a temple of Æsculapius with statues of Æsculapius and Hygiea by Scopas, and the river Lusius flows by it.

l: Lusius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Lusius is the local name for the river flowing by Gortys, named from the tradition that Zeus was washed there after his birth. People living farther away call it Gortynius, and it is described as one of the coldest streams, rising at Thisoa and joining the Alpheus at Rhæteæ.

l: Teuthis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Teuthis is a village near Thisoa and was formerly a town. Its associated leader, also named Teuthis, quarreled with Agamemnon, wounded Athene in the thigh while she appeared in the semblance of Melas, and returned with his Arcadian detachment; afterward, a wasting disease afflicted him and his land became unfruitful. The village has temples of Aphrodite and Artemis.

l: Athene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Athene tried to stop Teuthis from marching home from Aulis while appearing in the semblance of Melas the son of Ops. Teuthis wounded her thigh with his spear, and later the people of Teuthis made a statue of her with a wound in the thigh to propitiate her after oracular responses from Dodona.

l: Megalopolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Megalopolis lies along the road from Gortys, near a monument to those who fell in the battle against Cleomenes. Its people call the monument the Treaty Violation because Cleomenes violated the treaty.

l: monument to those who fell in the battle against Cleomenes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: The monument stands on the road from Gortys to Megalopolis and commemorates those who fell in the battle against Cleomenes. The people of Megalopolis call it the Treaty Violation because Cleomenes violated the treaty.

l: battle against Cleomenes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: The battle against Cleomenes is remembered by a monument on the road from Gortys to Megalopolis. The monument is associated with Cleomenes' violation of a treaty.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: After crossing the Alpheus, the traveler reaches Trapezus and then Bathos, where rites are held for the Great Goddesses every third year. The Arcadians say that the battle between the giants and the gods took place at Bathos, where they sacrifice to thunder, lightning, and storms. The text discusses Homer’s references to giants and argues that they were mortal rather than divine and did not have dragons’ feet. It also describes a giant corpse found in the diverted channel of the Orontes, which an oracle identified as Orontes of Indian race, before describing Basilis and Thocnia near the Alpheus.

l: Alpheus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: The traveler crosses the Alpheus after passing Trapezus and again after visiting Basilis. The Helisson eventually flows into the Alpheus.

l: Bathos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Bathos lies near the Alpheus, not far from Trapezus. Rites to the Great Goddesses are held there every third year, and the spring called Olympias and a ground fire are nearby.

l: battle between the giants and the gods, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: The Arcadians say that the fabled battle between the giants and the gods took place at Bathos rather than at Pallene in Thrace. They sacrifice there to thunder, lightning, and storms.

l: giants, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: The text presents the giants as mortal rather than divine and says that Homer described the Læstrygones and Phæacians in connection with giants. It rejects the fable that the giants had dragons instead of feet.

l: Homer, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Homer does not mention the giants in the Iliad, but in the Odyssey he compares the Læstrygones to giants and has the king of the Phæacians describe the Phæacians as near the gods, like the Cyclopes and the race of giants. The text also cites Homer as showing that the giants were mortal.

l: Orontes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Orontes is a river in Syria that runs through precipitous rocks rather than across a level plain. The Roman Emperor diverted it into a navigable canal, and when the old channel dried, a more than eleven-cubit earthenware coffin containing a perfectly formed giant corpse was found there.

l: Orontes of Indian race, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: The god in Clarus told Syrians consulting the oracle that the giant corpse found in the old channel of the Orontes was Orontes of Indian race. The text connects this identification with the claim that India produced mortals earlier or larger than other regions.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: The river Helisson rises in a village of the same name, passes through Dipæa, Lycæatæ, and Megalopolis, divides Megalopolis, and joins the Alpheus. Megalopolis contains a market-place with precincts, temples, porticoes, public offices, statues, and a council chamber. The unit describes the precinct and temple of Lycæan Zeus, along with monuments to Polybius and other figures. Polybius is honored for his historical writing, service to Rome, and role in helping Greek cities of the Achæan League establish constitutions and laws.

l: Helisson, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Helisson rises in a village of the same name, flows through Dipæa, Lycæatæ, and Megalopolis, and falls into the Alpheus about 30 stades from Megalopolis. It divides Megalopolis into two parts, and water from a spring on Mount Scolitas flows into it.

l: Megalopolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Megalopolis is divided by the river Helisson and contains a market-place, temples, precincts, porticoes, public offices, and a council chamber. Its people named the Philip’s portico after Philip the son of Amyntas to gratify him, and they erected the Myropolis portico from spoils taken from the Lacedæmonians. Megalopolis also honored Polybius with a statue on a pillar.

l: market-place of Megalopolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: The market-place of Megalopolis lies to the north, on the right of the Helisson’s course. It contains precincts and a stone temple to Lycæan Zeus, Philip’s portico, Hermes Acacesius’ temple, public offices, the Myropolis and Aristandreum porticoes, a temple of Zeus Soter, and the statue of Polybius.

l: Zeus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Lycæan Zeus has precincts and a stone temple in the market-place of Megalopolis. The temple has no approach, but its interior is visible; it contains altars, two tables, and two eagles.

l: Achæan League, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: The Achæan League is described as the organization into which Diophanes the son of Diæus first ranged all the Peloponnese. Greek cities that joined the Achæan League obtained permission from the Romans for Polybius to establish their constitutions and frame their laws.

l: Polybius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXX.
s: Polybius the son of Lycortas is represented by a statue on a pillar in the market-place of Megalopolis. An inscription says that he traveled over every land and sea, was an ally of the Romans, and appeased their wrath against Greece. He wrote the history of Rome and the Carthaginian war, and Greek cities in the Achæan League had him establish their constitutions and frame their laws.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: The west end of the portico contains precincts and temples dedicated to the Great Goddesses, Demeter, Proserpine, Aphrodite, and other gods. Damophon made several statues there, including those of the Great Goddesses, Hermes, and Aphrodite. The worship of the Great Goddesses at Megalopolis is said to have been instituted by Callignotus, Mentas, Sosigenes, and Polus as an imitation of the Eleusinian Mysteries. The temple of Proserpine admits women at all times but men only once a year, while a large temple houses the rites of the Great Goddesses.

l: the Great Goddesses, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: The Great Goddesses are Demeter and Proserpine, the latter being called Preserver by the Arcadians. Their precincts contain statues, temples, and associated figures, and their worship is celebrated at Megalopolis.

l: Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Demeter has a stone statue about 15 feet high in the precinct of the Great Goddesses. A small Hercules stands by her, and statues of Demeter and Proserpine about 3 feet high stand before a grove.

l: Proserpine, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Proserpine has a statue whose parts beneath the dress are made of wood, and it is about 15 feet high in the precinct of the Great Goddesses. She is called Preserver by the Arcadians, and a separate stone statue of her about 8 feet high stands in her temple.

l: Damophon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Damophon made the statues of the Great Goddesses and the statues in the temple of the Great Goddesses and of Aphrodite. The daughters of Damophon are said to be represented by two maidens carrying flower-filled baskets.

l: Friendly Zeus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Friendly Zeus has a temple inside the precincts. His statue, made by the Argive Polycletus, resembles Dionysus and shows him wearing buskins, holding a cup and a thyrsus, with an eagle perched on the thyrsus.

l: the temple of the Great Goddesses and of Aphrodite, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: The temple contains statues made by Damophon, including a wooden Hermes and a mostly wooden Aphrodite. Old wooden statues of Hera, Apollo, and the Muses from Trapezus stand before its entrance.

l: Aphrodite, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Aphrodite has a statue in the temple made of wood except for her hands, head, and toes, which are made of stone. She is surnamed Inventive because, in the account given here, most inventions come from her in word or deed.

l: the worship of the Great Goddesses, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: Callignotus, Mentas, Sosigenes, and Polus are said to have first instituted the worship of the Great Goddesses at Megalopolis. The worship is described as an imitation of the Eleusinian Mysteries.

l: the Eleusinian Mysteries, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: The Eleusinian Mysteries are presented as the model imitated by the worship of the Great Goddesses at Megalopolis.

l: the temple of the Great Goddesses, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: A large temple is built for several gods, including Hermes, Apollo, Athene, Poseidon, the Sun surnamed Soter, and Hercules. The rites of the Great Goddesses are celebrated there.

l: the rites of the Great Goddesses, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: The rites of the Great Goddesses are celebrated in a large temple built for several gods within the precincts.

l: the temple of Proserpine, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXI.
s: The temple of Proserpine stands to the right of the temple of the Great Goddesses and contains a stone statue of Proserpine about 8 feet high, with fillets throughout the base. Women may enter it at all times, but men may enter only once a year.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: The unit describes the part of the city beyond the river, including a remarkable theatre with a perennial spring and the foundations of the Thersilium, a council-chamber built for 10,000 Arcadians. It records temples, statues, altars, and ruins associated with Apollo, Hermes, Aphrodite, Ares, Dionysus, Hercules, Artemis, and Asclepius. It also describes a racecourse, a hill with sanctuaries, and unusually large bones said to have belonged to one of the giants summoned by Hopladamus to aid Rhea.

l: theatre, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: The theatre lies in the part of the city on the other side of the river and faces south. It is described as one of the most remarkable theatres in Greece, and it contains a perennial spring.

l: council-chamber, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: The foundations of the council-chamber lie near the theatre. It was built for 10,000 Arcadians and was called the Thersilium after its builder.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: Apollo had a joint temple with the Muses and Hermes, of which only a few foundations remained. A statue of Apollo stood there in the form of a square Hermes, and another Apollo was seated on a throne about six feet high in a separate temple under the hill.

l: Hermes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: Hermes had a joint temple with the Muses and Apollo, of which only a few foundations remained, and a statue of him stood there in the form of a square Hermes. A joint temple to Hercules and Hermes no longer existed except for its altar; Hermes was also represented as a square god among the Workers and was famed as Zeus's messenger who conveyed the souls of the dead to Hades.

l: temple of Aphrodite, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: Only the vestibule and three statues remained of the temple of Aphrodite. The temple stood near an altar of Ares and near the racecourse.

l: Aphrodite, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: Aphrodite had three statues at her ruined temple. One was called the Celestial, another the Common, and the third had no title.

l: racecourse, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: A racecourse lay beyond the temple of Aphrodite. One part extended toward the theatre, where there was a spring sacred to Dionysus, and another part was associated with a temple of Dionysus said to have been struck by lightning two generations earlier.

l: Hercules, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: A joint temple to Hercules and Hermes was no longer in existence except for its altar. Hercules was also represented among the square Workers and was famed for completing his many Labours.

l: hill, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: A hill lay toward the east, with a temple of the Huntress Artemis on it and precincts sacred to the Huntress Artemis on its right. Another temple stood under the hill, containing Asclepius as a boy and a seated Apollo.

l: Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: The Huntress Artemis had a temple on the eastern hill, described as the votive offering of Aristodemus. Precincts sacred to her also lay to the right of the hill.

l: Æsculapius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXII.
s: Asclepius had a temple and statues together with Hygiea. Another temple under the hill contained a statue of Asclepius as a boy, standing erect and about a cubit in height.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Megalopolis, founded with the zeal of the Arcadians and the good wishes of Greece, has lost its ancient prestige and felicity and is now mostly ruins. The deity and fortune are said to bring changes, reducing strong and prosperous places to weakness and ruin while favoring newer cities such as Alexandria and Seleucia. Examples include Mycenæ, Nineveh, Thebes, Babylon, Tiryns, Delos, and other formerly wealthy cities that have declined. Fortune’s power is also shown by the submergence of Chryse and the formation of the island Hiera, illustrating the instability of human affairs.

l: Megalopolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Megalopolis was peopled with zeal by the Arcadians and received the best wishes of Greece. It has lost its ancient prestige and felicity and is now mostly ruins.

l: Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Greece is described as having supported the peopling of Megalopolis through the best wishes of all Greece.

l: deity, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: The deity is said to favor change and to reduce everything to subjection, bringing formerly strong and prosperous places such as Megalopolis, Mycenæ, Nineveh, Thebes, Babylon, and Tiryns to ruin or diminished condition.

l: Fortune, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Fortune changes the conditions of strong and weak places, favoring newer cities such as Alexandria and Seleucia while reducing older cities. Its power is also shown by the submergence of Chryse and the formation of Hiera.

l: human affairs, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIII.
s: Human affairs are described as fleeting and unstable, as shown by the rise and decline of cities and by the disappearance or creation of islands.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The route from Megalopolis to Messene passes the temple of Maniæ, identified with the Eumenides, where Orestes was said to have gone mad after murdering his mother. Nearby places commemorate Orestes’s madness, healing, and cutting of his hair, while local tradition describes his pursuit by the Furies of Clytæmnestra before his trial at the Areopagus. The route then reaches the Alpheus, where the Gatheatas receives the Carnion. Hermæum marks the boundary between Messenia and Megalopolis.

l: Megalopolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Megalopolis is the starting point of the route described toward Messene. About 7 stades from it lies the temple of Maniæ, and Hermæum later marks the boundary between its district and Messenia.

l: Messene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Messene is the destination of the road described from Megalopolis.

l: Maniæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Maniæ is a place about 7 stades from Megalopolis on the road to Messene, containing a temple of some goddesses. The name is thought to be a title of the Eumenides, and the Alpheus is about 15 stades from Maniæ.

l: Eumenides, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The Eumenides are identified with the goddesses worshipped at Maniæ and at Ace. They were said to appear black to Orestes while driving him mad and white after he gnawed off his finger; he offered them expiations and sacrificed to the white goddesses, who were usually worshipped with the Graces.

l: Orestes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Orestes was said to have gone mad at Maniæ after murdering his mother and to have gnawed off one of his fingers there. He was healed at Ace, cut off his hair at the Shearing-place, and was pursued by the Furies of his mother Clytæmnestra before the trial before the Areopagus.

l: Ace, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Ace is a place contiguous to Maniæ where Orestes was said to have been healed of his madness. It also contained a temple to the Eumenides.

l: Orestes’s madness, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Orestes’s madness was said to have begun at Maniæ after the murder of his mother. It was associated with his gnawing off a finger and ended at Ace when the Eumenides appeared white to him.

l: the pursuit of Orestes by the Furies of Clytæmnestra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The Antiquarians of the Peloponnese said that this pursuit occurred before Orestes’s trial before the Areopagus. They said that Perilaus, rather than the deceased Tyndareus, accused Orestes and sought vengeance for the murder of his kinswoman Clytæmnestra.

l: Alpheus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The Alpheus is about 15 stades from Maniæ. The Gatheatas flows into it at a place reached from Maniæ, while the Carnion first flows into the Gatheatas.

l: Gatheatas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: The Gatheatas receives the Carnion and flows into the Alpheus. It rises at Gatheæ in the Cromitic district, about 40 stades from the Alpheus, near the ruins of Cromi.

l: Messenia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIV.
s: Messenia is one of the districts whose boundary with Megalopolis is marked by Hermæum. Hermæum contains a Hermes on a pillar.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: The unit describes roads from Megalopolis to Messene, Lacedæmon, and several inland places in Arcadia. It identifies Hermæum as the boundary between Messenia and Megalopolis and records statues and temple ruins associated with Despœna, Demeter, Hermes, Hercules, Artemis, Poseidon, and Callisto. It also reports the Arcadians’ claim that Belemina originally belonged to them, though the account is judged improbable. Several former towns and settlements, including Tricoloni, Zœtia, Paroria, Thyræum, Hypsus, and Phalanthum, are described as deserted or ruined.

l: Messene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: A road from Megalopolis leads to Messene. The road passes through places near the boundary between Messenia and Megalopolis.

l: Megalopolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: Megalopolis is the starting point for roads to Messene, Lacedæmon, Methydrium, and other inland places. Roads from it pass through the Alpheus valley and connect with sites such as Phalæsiæ, Tricoloni, and the territory near Hermæum.

l: Messenia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: Messenia borders the district of Megalopolis at Hermæum, near the temple of Despœna. The road from Megalopolis to Carnasium in Messenia follows the Malus and reaches the place where the Alpheus rises.

l: Alpheus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: The Alpheus has its rise at Carnasium, where the Malus and the Scyrus mingle their waters with it in one stream. A road from Megalopolis reaches the Alpheus after 30 stades and then follows its riverside.

l: Lacedæmon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: A road from Megalopolis leads to Lacedæmon, first reaching the Alpheus and then following the river to the Thius and Phalæsiæ.

l: Belemina, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: Belemina is about 20 stades from Phalæsiæ and has a temple of Hermes. The Arcadians say that it originally belonged to them and that the Lacedæmonians took it from them, though this claim is considered improbable.

l: Arcadians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: The Arcadians claim that Belemina originally belonged to them and was taken by the Lacedæmonians. Their account is judged unlikely because the Thebans would presumably have restored the territory if the claim had been just.

l: Methydrium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: Methydrium is 170 stades from Megalopolis and is reached by a road into the interior of Arcadia. A high road toward Methydrium passes near Anemosa and the mountain Phalanthum.

l: Tricoloni, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: Tricoloni was formerly a town founded by the sons of Lycaon. It still has a temple and a square statue of Poseidon on its hill, with a grove of trees around the temple, and it is connected by roads with several ruined settlements.

l: Arcadia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXV.
s: The roads described lead into the interior of Arcadia. The text identifies the land near Schœnus and the unnamed place beyond it as Arcadian soil.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: Methydrium lies 137 stades from Tricoloni and was built by Orchomenus on a hill between the Malœtas and Mylaon rivers.
