Its traditions concern Rhea’s protection of Zeus from Cronos at Mount Thaumasium, where Rhea’s Cave is restricted to women sacred to the goddess. A road from Megalopolis leads to Mænalus, passing several temples, tombs, and ancient sites. Mænalus has ruins of a town, temples, athletic facilities, and a mountain believed to be sacred to Pan.

l: Methydrium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: Methydrium is 137 stades from Tricoloni and was built by Orchomenus on a high hill between the rivers Malœtas and Mylaon. Before it was included in Megalopolis, its inhabitants were victors at Olympia. It contains a temple of Poseidon Hippius near the Mylaon, and Mount Thaumasium and Rhea’s Cave lie above the Malœtas.

l: Rhea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: According to the people of Methydrium, Rhea came to Mount Thaumasium while pregnant with Zeus and received protection from Hoplodamus and the other Giants in case Cronos attacked her. They say she bore Zeus on part of Mount Lycæeus, but that the deception of Cronos and the offering of a stone instead of the child took place at Thaumasium. Rhea’s Cave is on the mountain, and only women sacred to her may enter it.

l: Zeus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: The people of Methydrium say that Rhea bore Zeus on part of Mount Lycæeus and sought protection for him at Mount Thaumasium. They also locate there the deception of Cronos, in which a stone was offered instead of the child.

l: Mænalus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVI.
s: A road from Megalopolis leads to Mænalus by the river Helisson. Near Mænalus are the ruins of the town of Mænalus, traces of a temple of Athene, and courses for athletic contests and horseraces. Mount Mænalium is considered sacred to Pan, and nearby inhabitants say they hear Pan playing his pipes.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: The account describes the temple of Despœna near Acacesium, its porticoes, images, altars, sacred grove, and associated rites. The statues of Despœna and Demeter were made by Damophon from a single block of stone, with Artemis and Anytus standing beside them. The Arcadians worship Despœna above the other gods and perform secret rites in her Hall, where they sacrifice animals by cutting off whichever limb they happen to touch. Nearby are a temple of Pan, an altar to Ares, and temples or statues of Aphrodite, Apollo, and Athene.

l: temple of Despœna, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: The temple stands within a sacred enclosure reached from the temple of Artemis the Leader. It contains statues of Despœna and Demeter, their throne and footstool, an altar to Demeter, an altar to Despœna, and an altar to the Great Mother. A mirror beside the exit shows the statues and throne clearly but shows a viewer only obscurely or not at all.

l: Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Demeter is represented seated beside Despœna, holding a torch in her right hand and resting her left hand on Despœna. She has an altar in front of the temple, and the Arcadians say that Despœna was her daughter by Poseidon.

l: Despœna, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Despœna is worshipped by the Arcadians more than any other god. They say that she was the daughter of Poseidon and Demeter; her general appellation is Despœna, while her private name is Persephone, which the narrator does not write for the uninitiated. She is represented seated with a sceptre and a cist on her knees, and her Mystic rites are performed in a Hall and grove near the temple.

l: statues of Despœna and Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: The statues of Despœna and Demeter, along with their throne and footstool, were made from one block of stone by Damophon. The stone was said to have been found and dug up within the temple precincts after a vision in a dream. The statues were about the size of the statue of the Mother at Athens.

l: Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Artemis the Leader had a brazen statue near Acacesium, shown holding torches. Another statue of Artemis stands beside Demeter’s throne, wearing a deer skin and quiver, holding a lamp and two dragons, with a hunting dog at her feet.

l: Arcadians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: The Arcadians worship Despœna above all the gods and bring every kind of wood into her temple except pomegranate wood. In her Mystic rites they sacrifice whatever animal each person has, cutting off whichever limb of the victim he happens to touch rather than cutting its throat.

l: Hall of Despœna, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: The Hall of Despœna lies a short ascent to the right of her temple. The Arcadians perform her Mystic rites there and sacrifice victims in abundance.

l: Pan, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVII.
s: Pan has a temple reached by a staircase, with a portico and a statue that is not very large. He is said to answer prayers and punish the wicked, and in ancient times he reportedly gave oracular responses through the Nymph Erato as his interpreter. A never-ceasing fire burns in his temple.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Lycosura is described as the oldest town on earth and as a model for all later town building. Mount Lycæus, also called Olympus or the Sacred Hill by some Arcadians, is associated with the rearing of Zeus and contains sacred sites, rivers, games, and rituals. The Arcadians identify the local Cretea and the Nymphs Thisoa, Neda, and Hagno with Zeus’s upbringing, and they perform rites to bring rain during drought. The mountain also contains an enclosure, altar, and temples connected with Lycæan Zeus, Pan, and Parrhasian Apollo.
